prize_parts.citation: For the development of ionizable lipid nanoparticles that enable the delivery of nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: Ionizable lipid nanoparticles are a molecular-design achievement with a clear principle: a lipid whose pKa is tuned to be near-neutral in circulation and cationic in the acidic endosome, combined with controlled rapid-mixing assembly that traps nucleic acid at high efficiency. That principle is what made siRNA therapy (patisiran) and the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines deliverable in people. It is also the clearest case on the shortlist of a chemical discovery that changed what clinicians can actually do, and it is independently validated across many labs and products. The delivery vehicle was not covered by the 2023 Medicine prize, which recognised the nucleoside-modified RNA cargo, so the chemistry remains unrecognised.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Credit is spread over the Vancouver group (Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan), the MIT lipidoid work (Anderson, Langer) and company teams, and any three-person cut leaves out serious contributors. A second reservation is disciplinary: some colleagues may read this as pharmaceutical formulation rather than core chemistry, and the prize may feel adjacent to the 2023 Medicine award.

responses.point: Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics (B024) is a game-changing, cleanly attributed two-person method with four decades of independent adoption, and recognition is overdue.
responses.response: I agree with Johan that attribution and maturity are as clean as they get on this shortlist, and that is a real strength I cannot claim for B064. Where I differ is on what changed for researchers beyond theory. I accept the method as chemistry of the highest standard, but its reach into experiment and medicine is indirect, whereas the delivery chemistry changed clinical practice directly. For me the cleaner credit argues that B024 is safe, not that it is more significant, so I would keep it as a serious candidate for the committee without ranking it above B064.

responses.point: Ionizable lipid nanoparticles are an achievement in lipid self-assembly and phase behaviour, and she proposes Cullis, Anderson and Hope as the trio.
responses.response: Emma's framing helps, because the pH-dependent charge, nonbilayer phase behaviour and fusogenicity are exactly the physical chemistry that makes this chemistry rather than formulation, and I find it a persuasive answer to the disciplinary objection. On the trio I respectfully differ. Anderson's lipidoid libraries were an important screening advance, but the ionizable-lipid and rapid-mixing principles come from Vancouver, and Madden's microfluidic and loading work is central to the encapsulation concept. I would keep Cullis, Hope and Madden, while acknowledging that Anderson is the most defensible alternative and that this choice is contestable.

responses.point: Massively parallel sequencing-by-synthesis (B012) turned a laboratory chemistry into the tool underlying genomics, and the chemical core is Balasubramanian and Klenerman.
responses.response: I share Andrei's view that sequencing-by-synthesis is real chemistry with exceptional impact, and I ranked it third myself. His restriction to the Solexa pair is the cleaner attribution and better than my three-name list including Rothberg. My qualification is that Sanger and Gilbert already recognised the earlier generation of sequencing, which makes the committee's novelty argument harder here than for lipid delivery, and competing claims from 454, Lynx and Columbia remain unresolved.

responses.point: Bifunctional degraders (B046) open a new pharmacological modality with quantitative chemistry, but approval of a PROTAC drug is not yet established, so recognition may be slightly early.
responses.response: Heiner's point on maturity is the reason I keep B046 as an alternative rather than my first choice. The mechanism is well confirmed, but clinical proof is still maturing and the credit among Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli, Handa and others is crowded, with the PROTAC and cereblon molecular-glue strands arguably calling for different people. I would revisit B046 in a later round if the chair's summary shows the committee leaning toward a more forward-looking prize.

uncertainties: How the committee will apportion credit between the Vancouver group (Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan) and the MIT group (Anderson, Langer); I cannot verify priority and patent details from the supplied materials.
Whether a majority sees delivery lipid chemistry as core chemistry rather than pharmaceutical formulation.
Whether a prize so close in time and subject to the 2023 Medicine award on mRNA is seen as redundant.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: I have no connection to the nominees on the shortlist, and my work on peptide-nanoparticle biosensors and hydrogels is related in theme to nanomaterials but not to the credited people. Emma Sparr's lipid and self-assembly background overlaps with the subject matter, but that is not a recusal issue.
